channel.title: Psychology Daily · kaixinguor
channel.description: A psychology daily: social and behavioural science, clinical care and the technology of the mind.

item.title: Psychology Daily · November 18, 2026
item.description: All six items today come down to one question: who is in the denominator? Of 3,777 older French adults, only 1,540 entered the second phase, and a 38% dementia gap rests on a single loneliness question. In hour-long home videos of infants, the exaggerated faces that emotion research depends on barely appear, and a happy face fills 12% of the time a baby sees a full face. A 120-person exercise trial finished with 74 people and reported no effect size for cognition. A 20-person psilocybin trial missed its primary endpoint and found its signal at week eight. WHO's 93% counts only people who completed treatment. And an app used by 80,000 people reports its 80% in its own words. Read the denominator before the conclusion. 30 years, 3,777 older adults: only chronic loneliness raised dementia risk, by 38%, while occasional loneliness showed no link

item.title: Psychology Daily · November 17, 2026
item.description: All five items today ask the same question: whose mouth did this number come out of? In data on more than 30,000 offenders, moral motive was not something offenders reported about themselves — outside raters scored it. The thousand-plus memories supposedly unlocked by hit songs are text written by listeners, not a memory test. The −7.6 points and the 0.65 effect size in a 222-patient phase 3 come from a company's topline release; the paper is not out. Behind APA's seven practices sits a single self-report figure: fewer than 40% of affected workers know whether their employer has a policy. And an 801-person brain-training trial has an active control and untrained tests, yet still reports a p value and the phrase "about 6.7 years". The strength of evidence usually lives not in the conclusion but in two small lines about measurement and funding. Read those two first. Ten studies and 30,000 offenders: crimes seen as morally motivated respond less to punishment

item.title: Psychology Daily · November 16, 2026
item.description: Five items today keep returning to the same word: the average. In fMRI from 138 adults, autistic and non-autistic responses to film were nearly indistinguishable on average, with the difference living between individuals. In 102,684 users of a mental health chatbot, depression gains tracked how heavily people used it, while half of them opened it a few times and left. A 23-person pilot reports g = −1.42, a number far too large for a sample that small to honour. Resting-state scans from 186 people split insomnia-related mechanisms in bipolar and unipolar depression, leaving a dozen or so patients per subgroup. And 24 interviews in Nepal suggest heat breaks the water and the power first, and children's moods second. Averages point at a direction; getting to a person takes a different kind of evidence. Autistic and non-autistic adults watching the same films: group-level brain responses looked alike, while autistic participants differed more from one another — most visibly in the social brain

item.title: Psychology Daily · November 15, 2026
item.description: Five items today collide on one question: has the thing we already do ever been put in a comparison group? Four classroom accommodations that schools hand to children with ADHD did nothing across a 255-child randomised trial. Guided self-help rebuilt for autistic adults did work, at d=0.47 over a year of follow-up in 266 patients. Chronic loneliness went with blunted cardiac vagal regulation, but that remains a correlation. WHO handed countries an instrument for counting child mental health services, not a verdict on them. And UCLA's gene activation worked only in cells carrying the mutation. On the same street: some of it has been tested, some of it has only been believed. 255 children with ADHD, randomised: extended time, frequent breaks, standing desks and quiet corners did not improve classroom behaviour or quiz scores

item.title: Psychology Daily · November 13, 2026
item.description: All four items today run into the same problem: telling a change in people apart from a change in the instrument. Sleep regularity is recalculated from an average of 154 days of ring data per person, and short observation windows shrink the association. Campus mental health improves for a third year, while 7% of students now take support from a chatbot. Reports of sexual harassment double in six years, and the authors themselves cannot say whether incidents rose or disclosure did. And the ninefold hospitalisation gap for parents with intellectual disability is probably need and detection working together. The bigger the number, the more it matters where it came from. About 23,000 adults with 154 days of wearable data each: less regular sleep-wake timing goes with worse depression and anxiety

item.title: Psychology Daily · November 12, 2026
item.description: All five items today ask the same question: which layer are you measuring? Ask a child and a parent the same diagnostic interview and in 65%-98% of cases only one of them reports the diagnosis. Finnish registers covering 282,000 children put cumulative conduct-disorder incidence at 0.8% by age 12, with 40.6% comorbid ADHD. Of 113 digital mental health policies across 40 countries, only 14.2% are actually about digital mental health. Change the instrument, change the finding. 3,816 Chinese adolescents, two waves five months apart: phone-related impairment tracks later emotion-regulation difficulty

item.title: Psychology Daily · November 11, 2026
item.description: Today's thread is that broad labels are being broken into measurable pieces. PMDD is not one condition but three subtypes with different onsets; the value of an antidepressant is not only how fast it works but whether it holds; and the chain from gender norms to distress mostly breaks in the middle in 1,651 adolescents. The finer the classification, the more specific the point of intervention. 1,651 Ethiopian adolescents: most direct paths from gender norms to distress did not hold

item.title: Psychology Daily · November 10, 2026
item.description: All five stories today sit in the same narrow band: the effect is real, it is small, and almost every design is missing the one feature that would settle it. One lost hour of sleep adds two points to a phishing click rate. Across 14 countries, shouting and hitting both travel with toddler behaviour problems, but not in a direction the data can fix. A choir for 14 children has no comparison group. A 145-patient emergency-department model has just nine positive cases in its 30-patient clinician comparison. Small is not the same as useless — but it does decide who should pay for the fix, and how much it is worth. One hour less sleep moved simulated phishing clicks from 15.56% to 17.76%

item.title: Psychology Daily · November 9, 2026
item.description: Today's thread is that psychological states are becoming readable signals — and readability is not the same as usefulness. A 92-country survey of 53,799 people puts the lows among young adults and richer countries; the full Instagram archives of 415 students separate emotional from social loneliness; and Wuhan has turned “work smell” into an eight-department clinic that saw 30,000 visits in three months. The more signals we have, the more insistently the same question returns: does any of this change an outcome? A 92-country survey of 53,799 people: mental wealth is lowest among the young and in richer countries
